analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $6.50 an hour and automatically adjusts it with inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee with no cosponsors and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Bernie Sanders proposed raising the federal minimum wage to $6.50 an hour — about $1.35 above the $5.15 level set by the 1996 increase — starting after December 30, 1997 [S2][S3]. The bill also tied future minimum wage increases to the cost of living, so the wage would rise each year the way Social Security benefits do, instead of only when Congress votes [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce and received no further action before the 105th Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, roughly 10 million-plus low-wage workers at the time, would see an immediate raise to $6.50 an hour and automatic yearly raises thereafter, ending the pattern of the wage losing value to inflation between congressional votes [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $6.50 an hour beginning after December 30, 1997, up from $5.15 [S2][S3].
Indexes the minimum wage to the cost of living starting in 1999, using the same adjustment formula as Social Security benefits, so the wage rises automatically with inflation each year [S2][S3].
Automatic indexing would remove the need for periodic congressional fights, during which inflation erodes the real value of the wage floor [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with minimum-wage workforces — restaurants, retail, and other labor-intensive businesses — would pay higher wages, and some of that cost could show up in prices or reduced hiring; taxpayers are not directly on the hook [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers, mainly food service and retail

drawbacks.text: Employers paying minimum wage would face a 27% jump in the wage floor, and critics of minimum wage increases argue this can reduce entry-level hiring or raise prices at businesses with thin margins [S3].
A $6.50 floor set as a flat national rate would apply the same wage in low-cost and high-cost regions, which critics argue is a poor fit for some local labor markets [S3].
Automatic indexing takes future wage decisions out of Congress's hands, meaning increases would continue even in a recession when some economists argue a pause would help preserve jobs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivered a direct, sizable raise to low-wage workers and took inflation out of the equation permanently — a meaningful gain for the bottom of the wage scale. The costs fall on low-wage employers and potentially on entry-level job opportunities, a real trade-off economists debate. It was a simple, single-purpose bill rather than a sweeping overhaul, so its design risks were limited to the standard minimum-wage arguments.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which never took it up; the Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders introduced the Liveable Wage Act of 1997 on July 28, 1997 [S1][S3].
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S5].
No cosponsors signed on, and the committee reported no action; that was the last entry in the bill's history before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses with minimum-wage payrolls kept the $5.15 wage floor, which was losing real value to inflation each year it went unraised; workers at or near minimum wage gained nothing from this bill, though Congress did enact a two-step increase to $5.15 in 1996 before this bill was filed. The absence of indexing meant any future raise still required a fresh act of Congress, which in the following decade took ten years.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Representative, Vermont (Independent, caucusing with Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to raise and index the minimum wage; the sole sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Bill Goodling (R-PA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report.

against.name: 427 House members
against.role: All other sitting House members in the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no base of support beyond its sponsor.

against.name: Low-wage employer industries, notably restaurants and retail
against.role: Opposition to minimum wage increases and indexing
against.what_they_did: Hotel and restaurant lobbies have historically opposed minimum wage increases and automatic indexing in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors from either party, so no roll-call or sponsorship split is visible in the record; only the Independent sponsor appears on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: Restaurants are the largest minimum-wage employer; a $6.50 floor with automatic annual increases would raise their labor costs every year. Keeping the wage at $5.15 without indexing preserved the status quo that relies on periodic congressional inaction.
Retail, hospitality, and similar businesses paying near the minimum would absorb a roughly 27% wage increase, potentially passed to consumers through prices.
Workers at or near the federal minimum would have received an immediate raise and automatic yearly cost-of-living increases, the first such indexing of the federal minimum wage.
